reviews.question: A non-flow reversible process takes place according to V = 15/P m³, where P is in bar. What will be the work done if pressure changes from 1 bar to 10 bar? [Given ln(10) = 2.3025.]
reviews.explanation:
The process is PV = 15 bar·m³. Hence V₁ = 15 m³ and V₂ = 1.5 m³ as pressure rises from 1 to 10 bar.
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ and V₁/V₂ = P₂/P₁ = 10.
For the reversible non-flow process, work by the gas is
W = ∫[V₁→V₂] P dV = 15∫[15→1.5] dV/V
  = 15 ln(V₂/V₁) bar·m³
  = −15 ln 10 × 10⁵ J
  = −34.5375 × 10⁵ J = −3.45375 MN·m.
The negative sign indicates compression: work input is 3.4538 MN·m, matching (c).
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Given V = 15/P m³, P₁ = 1 bar and P₂ = 10 bar.
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
P₁/P₂ = V₂/V₁; V₁/V₂ = 10/1.
Non-flow work = ∫ P dV = ∫[10→1] (15/V) dV
= 15∫[10→1] (1/V) dV
= 15[ln 1 − ln 10]
= 15[0 − 2.3025]
= −34.538 × 10⁵ N·m
= −3.4538 MN·m
= 3.4538 MN·m (compression).
reviews.note: Recomputed using the actual endpoint volumes 15 and 1.5 m³. The printed integration bounds 10 and 1 give the same ratio and result, but are not the physical endpoint volumes; the full source calculation is retained.

reviews.question: Specific heat at constant pressure can be given as (where γ is the ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and constant volume, R is a gas constant, and J is the Joule constant):
reviews.explanation:
With heat measured in the older thermal units and R in mechanical units, Mayer’s relation is Cₚ − Cᵥ = R/J …(i), where J is the mechanical equivalent of heat. Also γ = Cₚ/Cᵥ …(ii), hence Cᵥ = Cₚ/γ.
Substitute into (i):
Cₚ − Cₚ/γ = R/J.
Cₚ(γ − 1)/γ = R/J.
Cₚ = γR/[J(γ − 1)], (a).
In coherent SI units J is unnecessary and Cₚ = γR/(γ − 1).
reviews.sourceExplanation:
We know Cₚ − Cᵥ = R/J …(i), and Cₚ/Cᵥ = γ …(ii). Then Cᵥ = Cₚ/γ. Putting the value of Cᵥ in equation (i):
Cₚ − Cₚ/γ = R/J.
Cₚ(γ − 1)/γ = R/J.
Cₚ = [γ·R/(γ − 1)]/J = γR/[J(γ − 1)].

reviews.question: Nitrogen at 25 atm and 37°C is contained in a cylinder of volume 10 m³. The cylinder is placed in a large container of 150 times the cylinder volume. The container is perfectly evacuated and insulated. The nitrogen gas is allowed to discharge and fill the container. Calculate the final pressure after the system has reached equilibrium.

Treat nitrogen as an ideal gas and include the cylinder and evacuated receiving space in one insulated rigid system. Q = W = 0, so ΔU = 0 and T₂ = T₁ = 37°C ≈ 310 K. With the stated receiving volume V₂ = 150V₁ = 1500 m³,
P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂,
P₂ = 25 × 10/1500 = 0.1667 atm ≈ 0.167 atm, (d).
If 150V₁ denotes only the receiving free volume in addition to a still-accessible cylinder volume, the total would be 151V₁ and P₂ = 25/151 = 0.1656 atm. The source uses 150V₁ as the final accessible volume.

P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
25 × 10/T₁ = P₂ × 1500/T₂.
P₂ = 0.167 atm.

reviews.question: A steel tank placed in a hot environment contains 5 kg of air at 4 atm and 30°C. A portion of the air is released till the pressure becomes 2 atm. Later, the temperature of the air in the tank is found to be 150°C. The quantity of air allowed to escape is:
reviews.explanation:
Given m₁ = 5 kg, P₁ = 4 atm = 405.3 kPa, T₁ ≈ 303 K, P₂ = 2 atm = 202.65 kPa and T₂ ≈ 423 K. The steel tank volume is taken as fixed.
From PV = mRT, with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K),
V = m₁RT₁/P₁ = 5 × 0.287 × 303/405.3 ≈ 1.0728 m³.
For the final state,
m₂ = P₂V/(RT₂) = m₁(P₂/P₁)(T₁/T₂)
   = 5 × (2/4) × (303/423) ≈ 1.7908 kg.
Mass escaped = m₁ − m₂ ≈ 5 − 1.7908 = 3.2092 kg ≈ 3.21 kg, (d).
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Given m₁ = 5 kg; P₁ = 4 atm = 4 × 101.325 kPa = 405.3 kPa; T₁ = 30 + 273 = 303 K; P₂ = 2 atm = 2 × 101.325 kPa = 202.68 kPa; T₂ = 150 + 273 = 423 K.
From gas equation PV = mRT,
V = m₁RT₁/P₁ = 5 × 0.287 × 303/405.3 = 1.072 m³.
Again from gas equation for final state,
m₂ = P₂V/(RT₂) = 202.65 × 1.072/(0.287 × 423) = 1.79 kg.
Amount of gas escaped = m₁ − m₂ = 5 − 1.79 = 3.209 kg.

reviews.question: When the valve of an evacuated bottle is opened, the atmospheric air rushes into it. If the atmospheric pressure is 101.325 kPa and 0.6 m³ of air enters into the bottle, then the work done by the air will be:

The source splits the displacement contribution into the fixed bottle boundary (zero) and the atmospheric free-air boundary (PΔV). The displacement work done by air. Diagram labels: valve, 0.6 m³ of air, initial boundary and final boundary.
W = ∫[bottle boundary] P dV + ∫[free-air boundary] P dV
= 0 + PΔV
= 101.325 × 0.6
= 60.8 kJ.

reviews.question:
Process is called reversible process if:
(A) A system passes through a continuous series of equilibrium states during process.
(B) These equilibrium states cannot be located on property diagram, cannot be joined by line as a path.
(C) These equilibrium states can be located on property diagram, can be joined by line as a path.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
reviews.explanation: A reversible process must pass through a continuous succession of equilibrium states, so (A) is true. Those states can be plotted on a property diagram and joined to form a path, so (C) is true and (B) is false. The printed combination is (A) and (C) only, (b). These are the quasi-static conditions necessary for reversibility; absence of friction and other dissipative effects is additionally needed, so the wording should not be taken as a sufficient definition of reversibility.

Process is called reversible process if:
(a) A system passes through a continuous series of equilibrium states during process.
(b) These equilibrium states can be located on property diagram, can be joined by line as a path.

reviews.question: The gauge pressure reading on an automobile tire is 240 kPa when the tire temperature is −30°C. The automobile is driven to a warmer climate and the tire temperature increases to 65°C. Assume the mass and the volume do not change. Then estimate the gauge pressure in the tire.
reviews.explanation:
The ideal-gas law uses absolute pressure. For fixed mass and volume,
(P₂,g + Pₐₜₘ)/(P₁,g + Pₐₜₘ) = T₂/T₁.
T₁ = −30 + 273.15 = 243.15 K; T₂ = 65 + 273.15 = 338.15 K.
Thus P₂,g = (240 + Pₐₜₘ)(338.15/243.15) − Pₐₜₘ.
For standard atmospheric pressure 101.325 kPa, this gives P₂,g ≈ 373.35 kPa, absent from all four choices. Even taking 100 kPa atmosphere gives about 372.84 kPa. The source obtains 333.8 kPa by applying P/T = constant directly to gauge pressures, which is invalid. Atmospheric pressure is also not supplied. No printed option is a valid unique gauge-pressure result.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Given (Pg)₁ = 240 kPa, T₁ = −30°C = 243 K; T₂ = 65°C = 338 K; (Pg)₂ = ?.
From ideal-gas equation PV = mRT, V and m are constant, P ∝ T.
(Pg)₂/(Pg)₁ = T₂/T₁.
(Pg)₂ = (338/243) × 240 = 333.827 kPa ≈ 333.8 kPa.
reviews.note: Printed key (b) and full original derivation retained. Correct absolute-pressure treatment gives no matching option and requires ambient pressure; this cannot be graded using the erroneous gauge-pressure ratio.

reviews.question: The heat transfer problems in which the temperature at a particular point in the system periodically reaches the same value belong to
reviews.explanation: If temperature at a fixed point varies with time and repeats after a period, T(x,t + τ) = T(x,t), the behavior is periodic unsteady heat transfer. It is an unsteady process, (d), because ∂T/∂t is generally nonzero. A steady temperature field is independent of time. “Quasi-steady” describes an approximation in which a slowly changing field is treated as a succession of steady states; periodicity alone does not establish that approximation. The source key (b) is incorrect, and its sketch is a monotonic approach to a plateau, not a periodic temperature history.

reviews.explanation:
The molar ideal-gas equation is PV = nRᵤT. Here Rᵤ = 8314 J/(kg-mol·K), T ≈ 300 K and P = 600 × 10³ N/m².

R̄ = 8314 J/(kg-mol·K); T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; P = 600 × 10³ N/m².
PV = nR̄T. V = nR̄T/P.
V/n = R̄T/P = 8314 × 300/(600 × 10³) = 4.17 m³/kg-mol.

reviews.question: At Pressure P and absolute temperature T, the mass m of an ideal gas fills a closed container of volume V. An additional mass 2m of the same gas is introduced into the container and the volume is then reduced to V/3 and the temperature to T/3. The pressure of the gas will now be
reviews.explanation:
If m₀ is the molar mass, initially PV = (m/m₀)RᵤT. After an additional 2m is introduced, total mass is 3m, volume is V/3 and temperature is T/3.
P′(V/3) = (3m/m₀)Rᵤ(T/3) = (m/m₀)RᵤT = PV.
Consequently P′ = 3P, (a). Equivalently P′/P = (3m/m)(T/3T)/(V/3V) = 3.

reviews.question: An insulated rigid vessel contains some gas and an electrical resistor. In a certain interval of time the resistor connected to an external electric power source heats the gas. Considering the vessel and its contents as the system,

options.a: Heat and work transfers are zero
options.b: Heat and work transfers are positive
options.c: Heat transfer is zero and work transfer is negative
options.d: Heat transfer is positive and work transfer is zero.

reviews.explanation: The system includes the insulated vessel, gas and resistor. Insulation gives heat transfer Q = 0. The fixed vessel gives zero moving-boundary work, but the external power source supplies electrical work through the wires. With work by the system taken positive, this electrical work input is negative: W < 0. Therefore heat transfer is zero and work transfer is negative, (c); ΔU = Q − W > 0.
reviews.sourceExplanation: An insulated rigid vessel contains some gas and an electrical resistor. In a certain interval of time the resistor connected to an external power source heats the gas. So, heat transfer is due to insulation and work done on the system, so, it is negative.
reviews.note: The source’s phrase “heat transfer is due to insulation” omits “zero”; the explanation here states the correct zero-heat result while preserving the full printed wording separately.

reviews.question: In which of the following processes, the heat is fully converted into work?
reviews.explanation: For the usual closed ideal-gas comparison, a reversible isothermal process has ΔT = 0 and therefore ΔU = 0. From ΔU = Q − W, Q = W: all heat admitted is converted to work during this process, (d). A reversible adiabatic process has Q = 0, isochoric (“isometric”) work is zero, and isobaric heating generally increases U. This is a single process, not a cyclic engine; complete heat-to-work conversion in a cycle from a single reservoir would violate the second law. The ideal-gas assumption matters because isothermal alone need not give ΔU = 0 for a real fluid. Reversibility also requires both system and surroundings to be restorable, beyond merely proceeding slowly.
reviews.sourceExplanation: Reversible means that, in principle, the process is done infinitely slowly so that the microscopic reverse from the final state exactly regenerates the initial state. So, in reversible isothermal process the heat is fully converted into work.

reviews.question: The heat capacity of the substance is given by expression:
reviews.explanation:
Heat capacity (thermal capacity) is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the specified amount of material by one unit, for a defined process. It is an extensive property, denoted C. If c is the corresponding specific heat and m the mass,
C = mc, with units J/K.

reviews.sourceExplanation:
Heat Capacity—Heat capacity or thermal capacity is a physical property of matter, defined as the amount of heat to be supplied to a given mass of a material to produce a unit change in its temperature. Heat capacity is an extensive property. It is denoted by C.
C = m × c (J/k).
Where m → mass of the system and c → specific heat.

reviews.question:
Which of the following are intensive properties?
(1) Density; (2) Pressure; (3) Energy; (4) Enthalpy; (5) Temperature.
reviews.explanation:
Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of a homogeneous system. Density, pressure and temperature are intensive: items 1, 2 and 5, (b). Energy and enthalpy without the word “specific” denote total quantities and are extensive.
Examples of intensive properties include pressure, temperature, density, thermal conductivity and specific energies. Examples of extensive properties include volume, mass, kinetic energy, potential energy, enthalpy, entropy and internal energy.
Density ρ = mass/volume is intensive because both numerator and denominator scale with system size. Specific enthalpy, specific entropy and specific internal energy are also intensive, as is specific volume. Heat capacity is extensive; specific heat capacity is intensive. A ratio of extensive properties is size-independent when both scale with the same system size. The source’s exception for “specific density” is not a valid general rule.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Intensive Properties: Properties independent of mass are known as intensive properties. Examples: pressure, temperature, density, thermal conductivity and all specific energy, etc.
Extensive Properties: Properties which depend upon the mass of the system are known as extensive properties. Examples: volume, mass, all forms of energy [K.E., P.E., enthalpy, entropy and internal energy], etc.
Note:
1. The ratio of two extensive properties are known as intensive properties. Density (ρ) = mass (extensive)/volume (extensive) → intensive.
2. All specific forms except specific density are always intensive properties. Examples: specific enthalpy, specific entropy, specific internal energy, etc.
• Heat capacity is an extensive property.

reviews.question: The measurement of elevated temperature is generally above 500°C. The instrument used for this purpose is known as:
reviews.explanation:
A pyrometer measures temperature remotely from an object’s emitted thermal radiation, so it is suited to elevated temperatures, commonly above 500°C: (b). A thermometer is the broader category of temperature-measuring instruments; a radiation pyrometer is a noncontact thermometer used for hot bodies.
The other supplied instruments have different functions: a manometer measures pressure; a potentiometer is a three-terminal variable resistor used as an adjustable voltage divider (and potentiometric instruments can measure emf); a tachometer measures the rotational speed of a shaft or disk; and a rotameter is a variable-area flowmeter for volumetric liquid or gas flow. The printed choice spells manometer as “Monometer”.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
• Pyrometer: An instrument that measures temperature remotely, i.e. by measuring radiation from the object without having to be in contact. The main difference between thermometer and pyrometer is that the thermometer is a device to measure temperature and pyrometer is a remote-sensing thermometer used to measure high temperature.
• Monometer: An instrument used to measure and indicate pressure.
• Potentiometer: Defined as a three-terminal variable resistor in which resistance is manually varied to control the flow of electric current. A potentiometer acts as an adjustable voltage divider.
• Tachometer: An instrument designed to measure the rotation speed of a shaft or disk.
• Rotameter: A flowmeter that measures volumetric flow of liquid and gases.
